# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Under comparable reaction conditions, catalyst identity and temperature/time will control target formation; I expect an intermediate temperature and sufficient hold time to outperform extreme heating because degradation may rise at harsher conditions. A reaction-stage HPLC measurement will distinguish conversion/selectivity trends.

## H2 [tentative]
For a biphasic contact near the dossier scope, X0 should give the highest single-contact product recovery, while X1 or X3 may trade recovery for purity. Multiple contacts/washes may increase purity at a recovery cost. This assumes the dossier indexing is reliable; early phase-resolved HPLC will test it.

Decision plan: screen reaction conditions and extractants, then replicate/refine the best complete process. I will require final purity at least 0.80 and prioritize final-assay recovery among qualifying batches.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for screened conditions]
Catalyst and solvent identity materially influence reaction-stage performance. At 350 K/1800 s, C3 in S0 gave the best of the four catalyst screens (HPLC event runner-operation-0075), while C0–C2 were lower-yielding and/or less selective (runner-operation-0025, -0042, -0059). Removing the added component and switching to S1 increased the HPLC yield/recovery to about 0.122/0.097 at 1800 s (runner-operation-0091); 3600 s increased them to about 0.198/0.205 with similar reported purity (runner-operation-0106). The component and solvent changes are confounded in this comparison, so the component-specific claim remains unresolved.

## H2 [supported in current scope]
X0 extraction followed by an organic-phase wash can reach the purity constraint: the 1800 s S1/C3 process with 0.010 L wash assayed purity 0.861 (runner-operation-0101). Halving wash volume after a 3600 s reaction improved recovery but purity fell to 0.727 (runner-operation-0116). Numerical differences support a wash tradeoff, but reaction duration is a confound and there is no replicate yet.

## Next tests
Screen S2 and S3 with C3/no added component at 3600 s, then refine the S1 reaction and wash volume near the purity boundary. Prefer the qualifying batch with highest final recovery; replicate the leading recipe if resources permit.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for screened conditions]
Catalyst and solvent identity materially influenced reaction-stage observations. At 350 K/1800 s, C3 in S0 outperformed C0–C2 in the catalyst screen (runner-operation-0025, -0042, -0059, -0075). C3 in S1 without an added component gave HPLC yield/recovery about 0.122/0.097 at 1800 s (runner-operation-0091), and extending to 3600 s increased these to about 0.198/0.205 (runner-operation-0106). Because removal of the component and solvent identity changed together relative to early batches, their separate causal contributions remain unresolved.

## H2 [supported in current scope]
X0 extraction and organic-phase washing produced the only assayed material meeting purity >=0.80: batch 6 assayed purity 0.861 and recovery 0.0334 (runner-operation-0101). The related 3600 s reaction with a 0.005 L wash had higher recovery 0.0585 but purity only 0.727 (runner-operation-0116). Thus the available evidence shows a purity–recovery tradeoff, though reaction duration confounds the wash-volume comparison.

## H3 [disconfirmed / unsafe scope]
S2 at 350 K for 3600 s did not preserve terminable material; the downstream extraction sequence failed and batch 8 was discarded (runner-operation-0121 through -0142). Do not generalize the S1 process to S2.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed batch 6 because it is the only completed final assay satisfying the mandated purity threshold and therefore dominates nonqualifying higher-recovery runs under the stated constraint. This decision would change if a completed batch showed purity >=0.80 with recovery above 0.0334.

## Campaign limitation
The shared reagent ledger was exhausted after treating add_component and add_reagent as independent charges in early batches. Consequently batches 8–12 were discarded rather than finally assayed; all 12 allowed nonfinal measurements were nevertheless used. This prevents a planned replicate/refinement and weakens uncertainty assessment.

payload.report:
Mechanistic report

1. Working picture of the world

I interpret the process as three coupled stages: catalytic conversion of a limiting reagent into target and byproducts; liquid–liquid partitioning of those solutes; and purification by phase selection, washing, drying, and sometimes concentration. The final objective is not simply high reaction conversion. It is high target amount in the selected final stream relative to the original reagent charge, with target purity at least 0.80.

A useful minimal state description is the amount of unreacted material R, target P, reaction impurity B, degradation products D, liquid volume V, and the phase containing each solute. A plausible reaction model is

  dR/dt = -k(C,S,T) R
  dP/dt = s(C,S,T,A) kR - kdeg(S,T)P
  dB/dt = [1-s(C,S,T,A)]kR + other side-reaction terms
  dD/dt = kdeg(S,T)P,

where C is catalyst identity, S is reaction solvent, T is temperature, and A denotes whether the additional component was charged. Catalyst and solvent appear to affect both the rate constant k and branching selectivity s. Temperature and residence time can raise conversion while also permitting byproduct formation or product loss.

At the reaction-stage HPLC measurements, yield was approximately conversion multiplied by selectivity. For example, batch 6 gave conversion 0.19697 and selectivity 0.63375, whose product is about 0.125, close to the measured yield 0.12225. Batch 7 gave 0.34144 × 0.59603 ≈ 0.203, close to its measured yield 0.19802. This supports a sequential interpretation in which conversion measures depletion of reaction-stage feed and selectivity measures the fraction of converted material assigned to target.

After quenching, I model extraction approximately by distribution equilibria:

  n(P,organic)/n(P,aqueous) = K_P Vo/Va
  n(I,organic)/n(I,aqueous) = K_I Vo/Va,

where Vo and Va are organic and aqueous volumes. The material dossier assigned X0 K_P = 2.585, K_I = 0.552, and K_P/K_I = 4.685 under its reference conditions. Thus X0 was expected to enrich target in the organic phase, but a single contact could not recover all target. Washing then introduces another purity–recovery tradeoff: it can remove impurity but can also remove target. Drying and concentration probably alter residual solvent and volume more than chemical composition, although the campaign did not isolate those effects.

Final purity is best understood as target divided by total selected solutes, whereas final recovery is target in the selected product stream divided by the original reagent charge. These downstream quantities are phase-specific. They should not be equated with the earlier reaction-stage HPLC estimates. In particular, final-assay conversion was near one in several batches even when reaction-stage HPLC conversion had been only 0.10–0.34. Phase separation can remove unreacted reagent from the selected stream, so this final conversion is not evidence that the reactor itself reached complete conversion.

2. Evidence for catalyst effects

Batches 2–5 formed the main catalyst screen. They used S0, an initial component charge, 350 K, 1800 s, and catalysts C0–C3 respectively before HPLC analysis. The reaction-stage observations were:

- Batch 2, C0: conversion 0.10175, selectivity 0.32958, purity 0.37670, yield 0.03458.
- Batch 3, C1: conversion 0.10265, selectivity 0.51747, purity 0.52888, yield 0.04447.
- Batch 4, C2: conversion 0.12217, selectivity 0.22065, purity 0.25091, yield 0.01388.
- Batch 5, C3: conversion 0.13108, selectivity 0.59934, purity 0.58652, yield 0.05448.

Within this narrow scope, C3 was the best catalyst: it gave the highest conversion, selectivity, purity, and yield of the four. C1 was second in selectivity and yield; C2 gave slightly greater conversion than C0 or C1 but converted material poorly into target. This shows that conversion alone is a weak optimization criterion.

These were single batches, not replicates. Nevertheless, several differences are much larger than the published HPLC noise scales of roughly 0.012–0.018 for the relevant channels, so catalyst identity is a credible causal variable. Exact rankings remain less certain because process variability was not independently estimated.

Batch 1 initially heated C0/S0 without the component for 1800 s and gave conversion 0.11214, selectivity 0.38894, purity 0.34112, and yield 0.03788. The component was then added and the batch was heated again. Because its charge timing and total thermal history differed, batch 1 is not a clean replicate of batch 2 and cannot identify a component effect.

3. Evidence for solvent, component, and time effects

Changing from the early S0/component-containing formulation to C3 in S1 without the added component produced the largest improvement observed at the reaction stage.

Batch 6 used C3, S1, no added component, 350 K, and 1800 s. HPLC gave conversion 0.19697, selectivity 0.63375, purity 0.60038, yield 0.12225, and recovery 0.09704.

Batch 7 used the same recorded formulation for 3600 s. HPLC gave conversion 0.34144, selectivity 0.59603, purity 0.59257, yield 0.19802, and recovery 0.20483.

Doubling time from 1800 to 3600 s increased conversion by a factor of about 1.73 and reaction-stage yield by about 1.62, while selectivity decreased from 0.634 to 0.596 and purity remained near 0.60. A simple first-order conversion model gives k ≈ -ln(1-X)/t of approximately 1.2×10^-4 s^-1 from either batch. That agreement is suggestive, not definitive: it comes from only two points and ignores catalyst deactivation, evaporation, and reversible chemistry.

The comparison with S0 suggests that S1 is a favorable solvent for C3, but solvent and component presence changed together. Therefore the campaign cannot determine whether the improvement came from S1, omission of the component, or an interaction between them. A plausible alternative is that the added component promoted an undesired branch or diluted the effective selectivity. Another plausible alternative is simply that S1 accelerated productive conversion. Those explanations remain experimentally unresolved.

Longer heating was not uniformly beneficial. Batch 5 continued for another 7200 s after its 1800 s measurement and ultimately assayed at only purity 0.33992 and recovery 0.02508. Batch 3 also received another 3600 s at 350 K and ended with purity 0.65508 and recovery 0.04683. These outcomes are consistent with overreaction or progressive impurity formation, but downstream recipes differed and final assays concern selected streams, so they do not establish a degradation rate. Batch 5's final degradation-warning channel was zero despite a byproduct signal of 0.05095, so the loss cannot be confidently assigned to the specifically labeled degradation pathway.

The only deliberate higher-temperature excursion was batch 2, which received 3600 s at 400 K after the 350 K HPLC measurement. Its final purity was 0.45239 and recovery 0.03711. Because catalyst, time, extraction, and temperature were all entangled, this does not identify a temperature law. It merely fails to provide evidence that the harsher treatment improved the complete process.

4. Extraction and washing

X0 was selected from the dossier because it had the highest nominal product/impurity distribution selectivity. The process generally added 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.030 L X0, mixed for 240 s at 700 rpm, settled for 120 s, and selected the organic phase. These volumes differ from the dossier's 0.030 L aqueous/0.018 L organic reference, so its numerical partition coefficients are only priors.

Batch 6 is the clearest successful complete process. After its 1800 s S1/C3 reaction, X0 extraction and a 0.010 L organic-phase wash produced final purity 0.86078 and recovery 0.03344. Final yield was 0.03137, impurity signal 0.01039, byproduct signal zero, and mass-balance error zero within the reported estimate. It was the only completed final assay satisfying purity ≥ 0.80.

Batch 7 used the 3600 s reaction and only a 0.005 L wash. Its final recovery increased to 0.05854, but purity was only 0.72673. Final yield was 0.06296, impurity signal 0.03192, and byproduct signal 0.02610. This supports a practical purity–recovery tradeoff: a smaller wash retained more target but left too much impurity.

The comparison is confounded because batch 7 also reacted twice as long and entered extraction with more target and more byproduct. It therefore does not quantify a wash coefficient. It only shows that the batch-7 combination of longer reaction and smaller wash failed the purity constraint, whereas the batch-6 combination passed it.

Relative to its pre-extraction HPLC recovery of 0.09704, batch 6 retained about one-third of that value in the final recovery channel. Batch 7 similarly fell from 0.20483 to 0.05854. Some reduction is expected from incomplete single-contact extraction, washing, phase holdup, and destructive analytical sampling. These ratios should not be interpreted as exact physical extraction efficiencies because the HPLC and final assay apply different observation contracts and include measurement noise.

X1 was used in batches 3 and 4, but the feeds and reaction histories differed from the X0 batches. Batch 3 finished at purity 0.65508 and recovery 0.04683; batch 4 finished at purity 0.50646 and recovery 0.01215. This is insufficient to rank X1 against X0 experimentally. The dossier's nominal selectivity slightly favored X0, but a clean matched extraction comparison was not completed. X2 and X3 were not tested as complete matched alternatives.

5. Solvent loss and failed S2 scope

Batch 8 used C3 in S2 without the component at 350 K for 3600 s. HPLC returned conversion 0, selectivity 0, purity 0, yield 0.01216, and recovery 0.01015. Subsequent extraction and termination operations reported that no terminable material remained, and the batch had to be discarded. The small nonzero HPLC channels are consistent with measurement noise around a material-depleted state rather than useful product formation.

This suggests either severe solvent/material loss, an unfavorable S2 process, or an operational state transition that removed the analyzable reactor contents. It does not reveal the chemical reason. Because S2 was tested once and no direct solvent-loss measurement was obtained, I would not claim a volatility constant. Operationally, however, the S1 recipe must not be extrapolated to S2 at 350 K for 3600 s.

Batches 9–12 contained only solvent after the reagent stock had been exhausted. Their HPLC signals were blank-like and they were discarded. They provide information about baseline/noise behavior but no valid reaction mechanism evidence.

6. Interpretation of completed final assays

The completed batches had the following final purity/recovery pairs:

- Batch 1: 0.60449 / 0.
- Batch 2: 0.45239 / 0.03711.
- Batch 3: 0.65508 / 0.04683.
- Batch 4: 0.50646 / 0.01215.
- Batch 5: 0.33992 / 0.02508.
- Batch 6: 0.86078 / 0.03344.
- Batch 7: 0.72673 / 0.05854.

Batch 7 had the highest final recovery among these, but it was infeasible because purity was below 0.80. Batch 6 was therefore the only observed feasible operating point, not necessarily the global optimum. Its recommendation follows the constraint rather than the native score.

Final mass-balance errors were small: zero for batches 2, 5, 6, and 7, and approximately 0.0030–0.0054 for batches 1, 3, and 4. This is reassuring about internal accounting but does not repair the lack of replication or identify where material was lost between reaction and isolated product.

7. Important couplings

The strongest apparent couplings are:

- Catalyst × solvent: C3 performed best in the S0 catalyst screen, and C3/S1 was substantially better than C3/S0. Other catalysts were not screened in S1, so the interaction surface is unknown.
- Time × selectivity: in C3/S1, longer time increased conversion and target yield but modestly reduced selectivity and did not improve reaction-stage purity.
- Reaction composition × washing: greater target production at longer time was accompanied by more impurity/byproduct burden, so the wash needed to satisfy purity may also have to be stronger.
- Phase ratio × recovery: distribution theory predicts that more X0 organic volume raises product recovery per contact, but it can also coextract impurity. Only one principal 1:1 added-phase ratio was tested.
- Temperature × solvent retention: the S2 failure indicates that thermal treatment cannot be optimized independently of liquid-volume stability.
- Measurement domain × interpretation: reaction-stage and final-stage conversion, selectivity, purity, and recovery are not interchangeable because phase selection changes the sampled material.

8. Unidentifiable factors and plausible alternatives

No process was replicated exactly, so run-to-run variability is unidentifiable. Instrument noise is published, but process variance is not.

The separate effects of S1 and omission of the component are confounded. The component may be chemically necessary, inert, or harmful under different conditions; the campaign cannot decide.

The temperature dependence of productive and degradative rates is unidentifiable. There are too few matched temperatures to fit Arrhenius relationships.

The extraction coefficients in the actual reaction mixtures are unidentifiable. The dossier may be correct, approximate, or misindexed, and matrix effects could change the effective K values.

Wash selectivity is unidentifiable because wash volume was changed together with reaction duration and feed composition.

Drying and concentration effects were not isolated. Their apparent lack of benefit in some batches may reflect the incoming material rather than those unit operations.

The S2 failure could be chemical decomposition, evaporation, phase bookkeeping, or another process-state effect. There is no direct measurement separating these alternatives.

The resource ledger was exhausted because early batches charged both reagent and the additional component from the shared reagent stock. Consequently only seven batches received final assays, while batch 8 and the four blank solvent batches were discarded. This prevented replication and a planned optimization near the purity boundary.

9. Best mechanistic synthesis and extrapolation limits

The most defensible synthesis is that target formation is a moderately slow, catalyst- and solvent-dependent conversion with branching selectivity near 0.6 under C3/S1 at 350 K. Over the observed 1800–3600 s interval, conversion behaved approximately like a first-order process while selectivity declined slightly. A longer reaction creates more target but also a more difficult purification burden. X0 preferentially moves target into the organic phase, and washing can raise purity above 0.80, but at a substantial recovery cost.

A plausible improved region—strictly an extrapolation, not an observation—would retain C3/S1/350 K and use a reaction time between 1800 and 3600 s, followed by X0 extraction and a wash between 0.005 and 0.010 L or a staged wash. The intended aim would be to approach purity 0.80 with more recovery than batch 6. This cannot be asserted as superior without an experiment because the wash response may be nonlinear and reaction impurities may change with time.

The report's mechanistic claims apply only to the anonymous benchmark materials, tested charge sizes, 350 K-centered batch conditions, and the specified virtual operations. They should not be interpreted as molecular identities or transferred to real chemicals. The firm empirical conclusion is narrower: among completed processes, batch 6's C3/S1 reaction, X0 organic extraction, and 0.010 L wash was the sole demonstrated way to satisfy the purity constraint.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the campaign because they use S2, C1 at only 0.00025 mol, 400 K, and— for Q07–Q12—a twenty-fold smaller reagent charge. I therefore used broad intervals, especially for long S2 heating: the only campaign S2 batch lost terminable material, although it used a different catalyst and temperature. Within each matched pair, the estimates follow the supported process relationships. Longer upstream time raises expected conversion and recovery but increases impurity or degradation risk (Q01–Q02). X0 has higher nominal product partitioning and selectivity than X2, giving Q03 modestly higher purity and recovery than Q04. A smaller organic phase preferentially enriches target but recovers less of it, whereas a larger phase recovers more impurity as well (Q05–Q06). Washing increases purity while sacrificing target recovery (Q07–Q08), and two staged washes should be more discriminating but more lossy than one wash of the same total volume (Q09–Q10). Concentration should mainly remove solvent, so Q11 and Q12 have nearly identical purity; Q12 has a small allowance for process loss. All recoveries include the 0.97 transfer fraction and a minor loss from the preceding destructive HPLC sample.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific optimum or authoritative mechanism prior was supplied. The material dossier provided nominal extraction coefficients, especially a prior that X0 should preferentially extract target over impurity, but explicitly did not provide an optimum process and could have been misindexed.

Supported:
- Catalyst identity mattered under the screened S0/350 K/1800 s conditions. Batches 2–5 gave reaction-stage yields of 0.0346, 0.0445, 0.0139, and 0.0545 for C0–C3, respectively; C3 was the strongest observed catalyst in that scope.
- Reaction-stage yield was approximately conversion × selectivity. This relationship held closely in batches 6 and 7.
- Longer reaction time increased conversion and target formation for C3/S1: from batch 6 at 1800 s to batch 7 at 3600 s, conversion rose from 0.197 to 0.341 and yield from 0.122 to 0.198, while selectivity declined from 0.634 to 0.596.
- X0 extraction plus washing could meet the purity requirement. Batch 6 reached purity 0.8608, consistent with the dossier's qualitative X0 selectivity prior.
- Washing involved a purity–recovery tradeoff. Batch 6, with a 0.010 L wash, achieved purity 0.8608 and recovery 0.0334; batch 7, with a 0.005 L wash and a different reaction duration, achieved greater recovery of 0.0585 but only 0.7267 purity. This is supportive but confounded by reaction time.

Contradicted or narrowed:
- My initial broad expectation that an intermediate temperature and sufficient heating would generally improve the process was too simple. Extended heating in batches 3 and 5 did not produce a superior final process, and batch 5 finished at only 0.3399 purity and 0.0251 recovery.
- Any implicit assumption that the S1/C3 behavior would transfer across solvents was contradicted by batch 8. C3/S2 at 350 K for 3600 s left no terminable material, so the process was narrowed specifically to the observed S1 conditions.
- Conversion alone was contradicted as a useful optimization target. Several final assays reported conversion near one while target recovery remained very low, because the final selected phase excluded other material.

Untested or unresolved:
- Whether S1 itself caused the batch-6 improvement or whether omitting the added component caused it. Those factors changed together.
- A genuine Arrhenius temperature law, degradation rate, catalyst-loading law, or validated kinetic order.
- Clean rankings of X0 versus X1–X3 under matched feeds.
- Independent effects of wash volume, wash staging, drying, and concentration.
- Reproducibility of batch 6; no exact replicate was completed.

The evidence that most changed my judgment was the C0–C3 screen in batches 2–5, the large improvement in batch 6, the time comparison between batches 6 and 7, and the S2 failure in batch 8.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would repeat the batch-6 reaction conditions—C3, S1, 350 K, 1800 s—but add the same component charge used in the early catalyst screen. I would take the same reaction-stage HPLC measurement and then use the batch-6 X0 extraction and 0.010 L wash so that both reaction and final outcomes could be compared directly.

The leading explanation is that S1 is the main reason batch 6 outperformed the S0 catalyst screen. The principal alternative is that omission of the component was the main reason.

- If the new reaction remained close to batch 6—roughly conversion 0.197, selectivity 0.634, and yield 0.122—and the final product again approached purity 0.861, I would strengthen the solvent-dominant explanation and regard the component as largely harmless under S1.
- If performance fell toward batch 5—reaction-stage conversion 0.131, selectivity 0.599, and yield 0.0545—I would strengthen the explanation that the component suppresses productive conversion or promotes an adverse interaction.
- If it lay between those results, I would infer contributions from both solvent and component or a solvent–component interaction.
- If it exceeded batch 6, I would reject the simple 'component is harmful' alternative and instead suspect that S1 and the component interact beneficially.

One batch would still not estimate process variance, but it would fill the most consequential missing comparison without changing several variables simultaneously.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

Unused or weakly used evidence included the raw HPLC and final-assay signal artifacts, detailed spectral shapes, control trajectories, and most cost and risk observations. I used processed estimates rather than reanalyzing raw traces. The nominal X1–X3 extraction anchors were also largely unused because there were no matched extraction experiments. Batches 9–12 were solvent-only, resource-limited discards; their small signals were useful mainly as qualitative baseline evidence and not for reaction modeling. Batch 1 was difficult to use mechanistically because its component was added after initial heating. I also lacked measurements of both separated phases, so extraction losses could not be closed directly.

The least reliable predictions are Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to S2 at 400 K and a catalyst loading twenty times below the campaign's main 0.005 mol charges; batch 8 gives a concrete reason to fear material loss in S2. Q07–Q12 are also uncertain because their reagent charge is only 0.002 mol, outside the campaign's productive-batch regime, and because wash staging and concentration were never isolated. The relative directions within matched pairs are more reliable than their absolute values.

The batch-6 recommendation is better supported than those extrapolations because it was directly observed and was the only completed batch satisfying purity ≥0.80. It is nevertheless not a demonstrated optimum and was not replicated. Its purity margin over the threshold was appreciable relative to final-assay instrumental noise, but unmeasured process variability remains.

The assigned goal clearly affected evidence collection. It encouraged rapid screening followed by extraction and washing aimed at meeting the purity constraint, rather than replication or a balanced factorial mechanism study. It also caused final recovery and qualifying purity to dominate the recommendation even though batch 7 had higher recovery. Early charging of both reagent and component exhausted the shared reagent stock, preventing planned replication and leaving five batches without final assays. Thus the campaign yielded a feasible recommendation but weaker causal identification than a mechanism-focused design would have provided. There was no unavoidable conflict between the goal and mechanism learning, but resource allocation created a practical one.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 6 is the only completed batch whose final assay met the required purity threshold (purity 0.8608 >= 0.80); its recovery was 0.0334. Higher-recovery completed runs failed the purity constraint, so batch 6 is the best feasible observed process.
